No, because $325 an hour is a reasonable rate under the Rule 1.5(a) factors.
Yes, because a lawyer may never raise her rate during a representation.
No, because the original agreement was in writing, so no further communication is needed.
Yes, because any change in the basis or rate of the fee must be communicated to the client.
oe: A lawyer may change her rates, but Rule 1.5(b) requires telling the client about the change.
Reasonableness is a separate question; the violation is the failure to communicate the change.
Mid-representation changes are allowed if communicated (and, under contract law, agreed to); they aren't forbidden outright.
The original writing covered the old rate; Rule 1.5(b) requires communicating any change.

Correct. Rule 1.5(b) provides that "any changes in the basis or rate of the fee or expenses shall also be communicated to the client." Billing a higher rate without telling Gil violates the Rule and may also breach the fee agreement.
questions.e: Rule 1.5(b): communicate the scope and the basis or rate of the fee and expenses, preferably in writing, and communicate any changes; a fee must also be reasonable under Rule 1.5(a).

questions.area: Limits on Fees, Retainers, and Fee Sharing (MR 1.5(a), (d), (e); 5.4; 7.2(b))
questions.q: Lawyer Hal flies to London for Client Ida's deposition and bills Ida for the eight-hour flight. During the flight he works on a brief for Client Joe and also bills Joe for those eight hours. Is Hal's billing proper?
o: Yes, because Hal actually spent eight hours on each client's behalf.
No, because a lawyer may not bill two clients for the same hours.
Yes, because Ida required the travel, and Joe benefited from the work.
No, because a lawyer may never bill a client for travel time.
Yes, so long as both fee agreements are hourly and in writing.
oe: He spent eight hours, not sixteen; billing both clients for the same eight hours charges one of them for time he didn't spend.

Correct. Charging two clients for the same time collects a fee for time not actually spent for one of them, which makes the fee unreasonable under Rule 1.5(a) and is dishonest under Rule 8.4(c). Burk Ch. 20 treats "double billing" as a classic billing abuse; the time should be divided or credited.
Both facts are true, but they justify dividing the time between the clients, not billing it twice.
Travel time can be billed if the agreement permits; the problem is billing the same time to two clients.
Written hourly agreements don't authorize charging for the same time twice.
questions.e: A fee is unreasonable under Rule 1.5(a) (and dishonest under Rule 8.4(c)) if it charges for time not actually spent for that client, as with double billing; overhead isn't billable unless agreed.

questions.area: Limits on Fees, Retainers, and Fee Sharing (MR 1.5(a), (d), (e); 5.4; 7.2(b))
questions.q: Lawyer Kai offers his paralegal, Lia, 10 percent of the fee from every new client she brings to the firm, in addition to her salary. Is the arrangement proper?
o: Yes, because Rule 5.4(a)(3) lets nonlawyer employees share in a firm's profits.
Yes, because Lia is a firm employee, not an outside referral source.
No, but only because the bonus must be approved by the clients in writing.
No, because it is fee sharing with a nonlawyer and payment for referrals.
Yes, if the total fee charged to each client stays reasonable.
oe: Rule 5.4(a)(3) covers compensation or retirement plans based on profit sharing, not a percentage of the fee from particular referred matters.
Rule 7.2(b) applies to anyone, including employees, who is paid for recommending the lawyer.
Client approval doesn't cure fee sharing with a nonlawyer or paying for recommendations.

Correct. Rule 5.4(a) bars sharing legal fees with a nonlawyer, subject to narrow exceptions, and Rule 7.2(b) bars giving anything of value to a person for recommending the lawyer's services. A percentage of each referred client's fee is both. Rule 5.4(a)(3) allows nonlawyer employees in a compensation or retirement plan even based on profit sharing, but not a cut of specific fees.
Reasonableness of the total fee doesn't fix the fee-sharing and referral-payment problems.
questions.e: Rule 5.4(a) bars sharing legal fees with nonlawyers except for payments to a deceased lawyer's estate, the purchase price of a practice, profit-sharing compensation or retirement plans, and court-awarded fees shared with a nonprofit; Rule 7.2(b) bars paying for recommendations.

questions.area: Limits on Fees, Retainers, and Fee Sharing (MR 1.5(a), (d), (e); 5.4; 7.2(b))
questions.q: Lawyer Mo and accountant Nan agree to refer clients to each other when appropriate. The agreement isn't exclusive, either may refer clients elsewhere, and Mo tells each client he refers to Nan about the arrangement. No money changes hands. Is the agreement proper under the Model Rules?
o: No, because a lawyer may never agree to refer clients to a nonlawyer.
No, because a referral agreement is something of value given for a recommendation.
Yes, because it is non-exclusive and the clients are told about it.
Yes, but only if the agreement is exclusive, so the clients' needs are met reliably.
Yes, without telling the clients, because no money changes hands.
oe: Rule 7.2(b)(4) expressly permits reciprocal agreements with nonlawyer professionals.
It is, which is why Rule 7.2(b)(4) carves it out as an exception when it is non-exclusive and disclosed.

Correct. Rule 7.2(b)(4) lets a lawyer refer clients to another lawyer or a nonlawyer professional under a reciprocal referral agreement "if the reciprocal referral agreement is not exclusive" and "the client is informed of the existence and nature of the agreement." Comment [8] adds that such agreements shouldn't be indefinite.
This reverses the rule: the agreement must not be exclusive.
Rule 7.2(b)(4) requires informing the client of the existence and nature of the agreement.
questions.e: Rule 7.2(b) bars giving value for recommendations except (1) reasonable advertising costs, (2) usual charges of legal service plans or qualified referral services, (3) buying a practice under Rule 1.17, (4) non-exclusive, disclosed reciprocal referral agreements, and (5) nominal thank-you gifts.

questions.tag: MR 1.15(c): advance fees go into trust
questions.q: Client Ola pays Lawyer Pat a $5,000 advance against hourly fees for a zoning appeal. Pat deposits it in his firm's operating account and plans to bill against it as he works. Is Pat subject to discipline?
o: Yes, because advance fees must be deposited in trust and withdrawn only as earned.
No, because the money will become his as soon as he does the work.
No, because a lawyer may deposit any fee he receives in his operating account.
Yes, but only if Pat spends the money before he earns it.
No, if Pat keeps accurate records of how much of the advance he has earned.
oe: Correct. Rule 1.15(c) requires a lawyer to "deposit into a client trust account legal fees and expenses that have been paid in advance, to be withdrawn by the lawyer only as fees are earned or expenses incurred." Putting unearned money in the operating account is commingling and risks conversion.
Until earned, the advance belongs to the client and must be held in trust (Rule 1.15(c)).
Only earned fees belong in the operating account; advances go into trust.
The deposit itself violates Rule 1.15(c); spending it would add conversion.
Good records don't cure depositing client money in the wrong account.
questions.e: Rule 1.15(c): advance fees and expenses go into the trust account and are withdrawn only as earned or incurred; earned fees must be withdrawn promptly so the lawyer's money doesn't stay commingled.

questions.tag: MR 1.15(d)–(e): third-party claims to settlement funds
questions.q: Lawyer Raj receives a $50,000 settlement for Client Sue. Sue's surgeon holds a valid statutory lien on the recovery for $12,000 in unpaid medical bills and has notified Raj of it. Sue tells Raj to pay her everything and "let the doctor chase me." What should Raj do?
o: Hold the disputed $12,000 in trust and promptly pay Sue the rest.
Pay Sue all $50,000, because Raj's duties run only to his client.
Pay the surgeon $12,000 at once, even though Sue disputes the lien.
Hold the entire $50,000 in trust until Sue and the surgeon resolve their dispute.
Return the settlement check to the defendant until the lien is resolved.
oe: Correct. Rule 1.15(d) requires prompt notice and delivery of funds to those entitled to them, and Rule 1.15(e) requires holding funds claimed by two or more persons separately until the dispute is resolved. Rule 1.15, Comment [4] says a lawyer may have a duty under law to protect a third-party claimant's lawful claim, such as a lien, against wrongful interference by the client.
Rule 1.15, Comment [4] recognizes that a lawyer may owe a duty to protect a third party's lawful claim, and Rule 1.15(e) requires holding the disputed amount.
Where the client disputes a claim, the lawyer holds the disputed funds until it is resolved; he doesn't take sides by paying either claimant.
Rule 1.15(e) requires prompt distribution of the undisputed portion.
Nothing permits returning the settlement; the funds belong in trust, with undisputed amounts distributed.
questions.e: Rule 1.15(d)–(e): promptly notify and deliver funds to the client and third persons entitled to them, hold disputed amounts in trust until resolved, and distribute the rest; a lawyer may have to protect a third party's lawful lien (Comment [4]).

questions.q: A celebrity athlete, Tad, is charged with assault and can't pay Lawyer Una's fee in cash. Una proposes that Tad give her the exclusive rights to a book about the case, to be written after trial, as her fee. Tad agrees in a signed writing after talking it over with an independent lawyer. Is the arrangement proper?
o: Yes, because Tad consented in a signed writing after getting independent legal advice.
No, because she may not get media rights to the case before it ends.
Yes, because the book won't be written until after the trial ends.
No, because a lawyer may never write about a former client's case.
Yes, if the value of the book rights is a reasonable fee under Rule 1.5(a).
oe: Those safeguards satisfy Rule 1.8(a) for ordinary business transactions, but Rule 1.8(d) bars this agreement during the representation regardless.

Correct. Rule 1.8(d) says that "prior to the conclusion of representation of a client, a lawyer shall not make or negotiate an agreement giving the lawyer literary or media rights to a portrayal or account based in substantial part on information relating to the representation." Consent and independent advice don't cure it; Comment [9] explains that the lawyer's interest in a good story could conflict with the client's defense.
The timing of the writing doesn't matter; Rule 1.8(d) bars making the agreement before the representation ends.
After the representation ends, a lawyer may negotiate media rights, subject to her continuing duties under Rule 1.9(c).
Reasonableness doesn't cure an arrangement that Rule 1.8(d) prohibits outright.
questions.e: Rule 1.8(d) bars making or negotiating an agreement for literary or media rights to the representation before it concludes; the ban isn't waivable, and under Rule 1.8(k) it applies to the whole firm.

questions.q: Lawyer Vic represents twelve homeowners suing a developer over defective foundations. The developer offers $1.2 million to settle all twelve claims, to be divided as Vic sees fit. Vic proposes a division, tells each client only his or her own share, and gets each client's oral approval. Is Vic subject to discipline?
o: No, because each client approved his or her own share of the settlement before it was accepted.
No, because the developer authorized Vic to divide the money as he saw fit.
Yes, because a lawyer may never settle the claims of multiple clients together.
No, if Vic's proposed division was fair to every client.
Yes, because each client must know all shares and consent in a signed writing.
oe: Each client must know what every other client gets, and consent must be in a writing signed by the client (Rule 1.8(g)).
The other side can't authorize the lawyer to decide his clients' shares; the clients must each give informed consent.
Aggregate settlements are permitted when Rule 1.8(g)'s requirements are met.
Fairness of the division doesn't replace the disclosure and signed-consent requirements.

Correct. Rule 1.8(g) bars a lawyer representing two or more clients from making an aggregate settlement "unless each client gives informed consent, in a writing signed by the client." The disclosure must include "the existence and nature of all the claims" and "the participation of each person in the settlement." Oral approval of one's own share isn't enough.
questions.e: Rule 1.8(g): an aggregate settlement of two or more clients' claims requires each client's informed consent, in a writing signed by the client, after disclosure of all the claims and each person's participation.

questions.q: Lawyer Wyn's engagement letter for a small-business client, Xu, says that Wyn's liability for any malpractice will be capped at the fees Xu pays. Xu, who has no other lawyer, signs it. Is the clause proper?
o: Yes, because Xu read and signed the engagement letter before Wyn began any work.
Yes, because the cap is reasonable in relation to the modest fees Xu pays for the work.
No, because a lawyer may never limit malpractice liability in any way.
No, because Xu was not independently represented in making the agreement.
Yes, if Wyn advised Xu in writing that he could consult another lawyer.
oe: A signature isn't enough; Rule 1.8(h)(1) requires independent representation of the client in making the agreement.
Rule 1.8(h)(1) doesn't turn on the reasonableness of the cap.
Rule 1.8(h)(1) permits such agreements when the client is independently represented, and Rule 1.8, Comment [17] notes that practicing as a limited-liability entity is permitted.

Correct. Rule 1.8(h)(1) says a lawyer shall not "make an agreement prospectively limiting the lawyer's liability to a client for malpractice unless the client is independently represented in making the agreement." Xu had no other lawyer.
Written advice to seek counsel is the standard for settling an existing claim under Rule 1.8(h)(2); a prospective limit requires actual independent representation.
questions.e: Rule 1.8(h): (1) no prospective limit on malpractice liability unless the client is independently represented in making the agreement; (2) no settling a malpractice claim with an unrepresented client or former client without written advice to seek counsel and a reasonable opportunity to do so.

questions.tag: MR 1.8(i): proprietary interest in the litigation
questions.q: Lawyer Yan represents Client Zora in a quiet-title suit over a valuable parcel. To help Zora pay her bills, Yan buys a 25 percent interest in the disputed parcel from her for a fair price, after giving her the written disclosures and advice Rule 1.8(a) requires and getting her signed consent. Is Yan subject to discipline?
o: No, because Yan complied with every requirement of Rule 1.8(a) for business transactions.
No, because the price was fair and helped the client pay her bills.
Yes, because it is improper financial assistance under Rule 1.8(e).
No, because a contingent fee also gives a lawyer an interest in the outcome.
Yes, because he bought an interest in the property he is litigating over.
oe: Rule 1.8(a) governs permitted transactions; Rule 1.8(i) independently forbids this one.
Fairness and good motive don't matter under Rule 1.8(i); the interest in the litigated property is the problem.
Buying the interest is the proprietary-interest problem of Rule 1.8(i); Rule 1.8(e) concerns loans and gifts for living expenses.
A reasonable contingent fee in a civil case is one of Rule 1.8(i)'s two express exceptions; buying part of the property isn't.

Correct. Rule 1.8(i) forbids acquiring "a proprietary interest in the cause of action or subject matter of litigation the lawyer is conducting for a client," except a lien authorized by law and a reasonable contingent fee in a civil case. Complying with Rule 1.8(a) doesn't cure it.
questions.e: Rule 1.8(i) bars acquiring a proprietary interest in the cause of action or subject matter of litigation, except (1) a lien authorized by law to secure fees or expenses and (2) a reasonable contingent fee in a civil case; Rule 1.8(k) imputes it to the firm.

questions.area: Concurrent Clients: The Concurrent Client Rule (MR 1.7)
questions.q: Law Firm Alder represents Small Co. in a minor trademark matter. Big Co., a much larger potential client, asks Alder to sue Small Co. in an unrelated patent case. Alder sends Small Co. a letter ending their relationship so that Small Co. will be a former client, then files Big Co.'s suit. Small Co. moves to disqualify. What is the most likely result?
o: No disqualification, because Small Co. is now a former client and the matters are unrelated.
No disqualification, because a client relationship ends whenever the lawyer sends a termination letter.
Disqualification, because a firm may never be adverse to a former client in any matter.
No disqualification, if Alder screens the trademark lawyers from the patent case.
Disqualification, because a firm can't drop a client like a hot potato to turn it into a former client.
oe: That is the result the firm tried to engineer; courts generally don't let a firm convert a current client into a former one for this purpose.
A firm may withdraw under Rule 1.16, but withdrawing to take an adverse matter doesn't change the conflict analysis.
Adversity to a true former client is barred only in the same or substantially related matters (Rule 1.9(a)); the problem is that Small Co. is treated as current.
Screening doesn't cure a current-client conflict, which is imputed to everyone in the firm under Rule 1.10(a).

Correct. Under the "hot-potato" rule Burk discusses in Ch. 22.B, courts generally treat a client dropped in order to take an adverse matter as a current client, so the Rule 1.7(a)(1) direct-adversity analysis applies. Small Co. hasn't consented.
questions.e: Hot-potato rule: a lawyer can't drop a current client to take a matter adverse to it and then treat it as a former client; the conflict is analyzed under Rule 1.7, not Rule 1.9.

questions.area: Concurrent Clients: The Concurrent Client Rule (MR 1.7)
questions.q: Brothers Al and Bo are charged together with burglary. They ask Lawyer Cara to represent both. Each says the other had nothing to do with it, and each may be offered a deal to testify against the other. Which statement best describes Cara's situation?
o: She ordinarily should decline, because the risk of conflict between criminal co-defendants is grave.
She may represent both, because their interests are identical: both want acquittal.
She may represent both if each gives informed consent, confirmed in writing.
She may never represent two co-defendants, because the conflict is nonconsentable under Rule 1.7(b)(3).
She may represent both, but must withdraw from both as soon as either is offered a plea deal.
oe: Correct. Rule 1.7, Comment [23] says "the potential for conflict of interest in representing multiple defendants in a criminal case is so grave that ordinarily a lawyer should decline to represent more than one co-defendant." The possibility of a deal to testify against each other is the classic danger.
Shared hopes don't remove the risks: differing defenses, plea offers and testimony against each other create a Rule 1.7(a)(2) conflict.
Consent requires a reasonable belief that she can represent each diligently (Rule 1.7(b)(1)); Comment [23] says that ordinarily she can't in this setting.
Rule 1.7(b)(3) bars claims between clients in the same litigation; co-defendants aren't asserting claims against each other, so joint representation isn't absolutely barred.
Starting a representation that is likely to collapse in this way is what Comment [23] warns against.
questions.e: Joint representation of criminal co-defendants is a Rule 1.7(a)(2) conflict that is ordinarily too grave to undertake (Rule 1.7, Comment [23]); co-parties in civil cases are judged by the same material-limitation test.

questions.area: Concurrent Clients: The Concurrent Client Rule (MR 1.7)
questions.q: Law Firm Dove represents Parent Inc. in tax matters. Another client asks Dove to sue Sub LLC, a separately managed subsidiary of Parent, for breach of a supply contract. Dove has no understanding with Parent that its affiliates would be treated as clients, and the suit won't affect Dove's work for Parent. Does representing the other client in the suit against Sub require Parent's consent?
o: Yes, because a parent and its subsidiary are always treated as a single client.
Yes, because suing a subsidiary is direct adversity to its parent.
Ordinarily not, because representing a corporation doesn't make its affiliates clients.
No, because the tax matters and the contract suit are unrelated.
Yes, unless Dove screens its tax lawyers from the contract suit.
oe: Comment [34] rejects automatic treatment of affiliates as one client; it depends on the circumstances.
Unless the affiliate is itself a client, the suit isn't direct adversity to Parent; at most a material-limitation question could arise.

Correct. Rule 1.7, Comment [34] says a lawyer for an organization doesn't, by virtue of that representation, necessarily represent its affiliates, such as a parent or subsidiary. Absent circumstances making the affiliate a client (an understanding, or the affiliates being treated as one) or a material limitation, the suit isn't direct adversity to the client.
Unrelatedness is the former-client test of Rule 1.9; the reason no consent is needed here is that Sub isn't a client.
Screening isn't the question; whether Sub is a client is.
questions.e: Representing an organization doesn't make its affiliates clients (Rule 1.7, Comment [34]) unless the circumstances, such as an understanding or shared management, make them so, or the work for one materially limits the work for the other.

questions.area: Concurrent Clients: The Concurrent Client Rule (MR 1.7)
questions.q: Lawyer Eve represents two coffee shops on the same block, Grind and Brew, in unrelated matters: Grind's lease renewal and Brew's trademark registration. They compete fiercely for customers. Neither has consented to Eve representing the other. Is there a conflict of interest?
o: Yes, because Grind and Brew compete, so their interests are directly adverse.
Yes, because a lawyer may never represent two businesses in the same market.
No, but only if Eve gets both clients' informed consent in writing.
Yes, unless Eve charges each client a different hourly rate.
No, because mere business competition isn't direct adversity.
oe: Economic competition isn't direct adversity under Rule 1.7(a)(1) (Comment [6]).
No rule forbids it; Comment [6] treats it as ordinarily permissible.
If there's no conflict, no consent is needed.
Billing has nothing to do with whether a conflict exists.

Correct. Rule 1.7, Comment [6] says "simultaneous representation in unrelated matters of clients whose interests are only economically adverse, such as representation of competing economic enterprises in unrelated litigation, does not ordinarily constitute a conflict of interest."
questions.e: Direct adversity means acting against a current client (suing it, cross-examining it, negotiating against it); mere economic competition between clients in unrelated matters ordinarily isn't a conflict (Rule 1.7, Comment [6]).

questions.area: Former and Prospective Clients: The Successive Client Rule (MR 1.9, 1.18(c))
questions.q: While Lawyer Fritz was an associate at Firm Gale, other Gale lawyers represented Hollis Corp. in a contract dispute. Fritz never worked on the Hollis matter and learned nothing about it. Fritz has since moved to a new firm, which is asked to sue Hollis in a substantially related matter. May Fritz work on the new case?
o: No, because a lawyer is bound by all the conflicts of his former firm.
No, because Hollis was his firm's client while he worked there.
Yes, but only if his new firm screens him from the case.
No, unless Hollis gives informed consent, confirmed in writing.
Yes, because he learned nothing about Hollis at his old firm.
oe: After he leaves, a lawyer carries his former firm's conflicts only where Rule 1.9(b) applies, which requires that he acquired material protected information.
Being at the firm isn't enough; Rule 1.9(b) asks what he actually learned.
Screening matters when a lawyer is disqualified; Fritz isn't, so he needs no screen.
Consent is needed only if a Rule 1.9 conflict exists; Fritz has none.

Correct. Rule 1.9(b) bars a lawyer from representing a person adverse to a client of his former firm in the same or a substantially related matter only if he "acquired information protected by Rules 1.6 and 1.9(c) that is material to the matter." Fritz acquired none.
questions.e: Rule 1.9(b): a lawyer who moves firms is disqualified from matters adverse to his old firm's clients only if the matter is the same or substantially related and he personally acquired material information protected by Rules 1.6 and 1.9(c) (Comments [5]–[6]).

questions.area: Former and Prospective Clients: The Successive Client Rule (MR 1.9, 1.18(c))
questions.tag: MR 1.9, Comment [3]: general knowledge vs. specific facts
questions.q: For ten years Lawyer Ivy defended Jett Corp. in employment cases and came to know its general management style and how it tends to approach litigation. Five years after her last Jett case, Ivy is asked to represent a former Jett employee in a new, unrelated wrongful-termination claim against Jett. Is Ivy barred by Rule 1.9(a)?
o: Yes, because any lawyer who long represented a client knows its "playbook" and is barred from opposing it.
Not ordinarily, because general playbook knowledge usually isn't enough.
Yes, because suing a former client is always prohibited.
No, because five years have passed, so all information Ivy learned is now generally known.
No, because the employee is an individual and Jett is an organization.
oe: Comment [3] treats general knowledge of policies and practices as ordinarily insufficient; the bar requires specific relevant facts.

Correct. Rule 1.9, Comment [3] says that for an organizational client, "general knowledge of the client's policies and practices ordinarily will not preclude a subsequent representation," while knowledge of specific facts relevant to the new matter ordinarily will. Burk calls this the "playbook" problem and notes that courts vary on close cases.
Rule 1.9(a) bars only the same or substantially related matters.
Time can make information stale, but it isn't the reason; the reason is that her knowledge is general, not specific to this claim.
The kinds of parties don't matter; the question is whether the matters are substantially related.
questions.e: Matters are substantially related if they involve the same transaction or dispute or there's a substantial risk that confidential information from the first would materially advance the new client's position (Rule 1.9, Comment [3]); general "playbook" knowledge ordinarily isn't enough.

questions.area: Former and Prospective Clients: The Successive Client Rule (MR 1.9, 1.18(c))
questions.tag: MR 1.9, Comment [3]: different-looking but related matters
questions.q: Lawyer Kurt helped Client Lars, a businessman, restructure his companies and learned all the details of his personal finances and hidden holdings. That work ended last year. Lars's wife now asks Kurt to represent her in divorcing Lars. Lars objects. May Kurt represent the wife?
o: No, because the matters are substantially related given the financial information he learned.
Yes, because a business restructuring and a divorce are different kinds of legal matters.
Yes, if Kurt promises not to use anything he learned about Lars's finances.
No, because a lawyer may never represent the spouse of a former client.
Yes, because Kurt's duties to Lars ended when the restructuring ended.
oe: Correct. Rule 1.9, Comment [3] gives nearly this example: a lawyer who has represented a businessperson and learned extensive private financial information may not then represent that person's spouse in seeking a divorce. There's a substantial risk the information would materially advance the wife's position.
Matters can be substantially related even if their legal claims differ; the question is the risk that confidential information would advance the new client's position.
A promise doesn't cure a Rule 1.9(a) conflict; only Lars's informed consent, confirmed in writing, does.
Too broad; only the same or substantially related matters are barred.
Duties to former clients continue under Rule 1.9.
questions.e: Under Rule 1.9(a) and Comment [3], matters are substantially related when confidential information from the first would materially advance the new client's position, as in representing a former client's spouse in a divorce after learning his private finances.

questions.q: Paralegal Mia worked on the plaintiff's side of a pending fraud case at her old firm. She takes a job at Firm Nash, which represents the defendant in the same case. Nash immediately isolates her from the case and instructs everyone not to discuss it with her. Is Nash disqualified?
o: Yes, because Mia's knowledge of the plaintiff's case is imputed to every lawyer at Nash.
Yes, unless the plaintiff gives informed consent, confirmed in writing.
No, because paralegals have no duty of confidentiality to their former employers' clients.
No, because a nonlawyer's conflict isn't imputed to the firm, though she must be screened.
No, but only if Mia is apportioned no part of the fee from the case.
oe: Comment [4] says nonlawyers' conflicts aren't imputed under Rule 1.10(a), provided they are screened.
Consent isn't needed when the firm properly screens a nonlawyer.
Nonlawyers are expected to protect confidences, and firms must supervise them (Rule 5.3); screening protects the former client's information.

Correct. Rule 1.10, Comment [4] says Rule 1.10(a) doesn't prohibit representation by others in the firm where the person prohibited is a nonlawyer, such as a paralegal or legal secretary, but such persons "ordinarily must be screened from any personal participation in the matter." Nash did that.
The fee bar is part of lateral-lawyer screening under Rule 1.10(a)(2); for nonlawyers, Comment [4] requires screening from participation.
questions.e: Conflicts of nonlawyer staff (and of lawyers based on work done before they became lawyers) aren't imputed under Rule 1.10(a), but they ordinarily must be screened (Rule 1.10, Comment [4]; Rule 5.3).

questions.tag: MR 1.10(c): client waiver of imputed conflicts
questions.q: Lawyer Ora's partner, Pete, represents Client Quay. Ora is asked to represent a new client in a matter adverse to Quay. The firm reasonably believes Ora can represent the new client competently and diligently while Pete continues for Quay. How may the firm proceed?
o: With each affected client's informed consent, confirmed in writing.
By screening Ora from Pete, without any client consent.
It may not proceed, because an imputed conflict can never be waived.
With Quay's consent alone, because Quay is the client being opposed.
By having Ora, rather than Pete, give her own written consent to the conflict.
oe: Correct. Rule 1.10(c) says a disqualification prescribed by Rule 1.10 "may be waived by the affected client under the conditions stated in Rule 1.7." Here the conflict is direct adversity to a current client, so each affected client must give informed consent, confirmed in writing, under Rule 1.7(b).
Screening without consent works only for the lateral-lawyer conflicts in Rule 1.10(a)(2), not for a current-client conflict.
Rule 1.10(c) expressly allows waiver by the affected client under Rule 1.7.
Rule 1.7(b)(4) requires informed consent from each affected client, which includes the new client.
Lawyers can't consent on behalf of their clients; the affected clients must consent.
questions.e: Imputed conflicts may be waived by the affected clients under Rule 1.7's conditions (Rule 1.10(c)); without consent, only Rule 1.10(a)'s personal-interest and lateral-screening exceptions avoid imputation.

questions.q: Lawyer Rae drafts estate documents for Client Sid. Rae's law partner, Ted, is not Sid's relative. Sid asks Rae to include in his will a $250,000 bequest to Ted, whom he admires. Rae drafts the will as asked. Is Rae subject to discipline?
o: No, because the gift goes to Ted, not to Rae, the lawyer who drafted the will.
No, because Sid chose the gift himself and Rae didn't solicit it.
Yes, because the gift-instrument rule applies to every lawyer in the firm.
Yes, but only because Ted, as a partner, should have drafted the will himself.
No, if Sid gives informed consent, confirmed in writing, to the gift.
oe: Rule 1.8(k) extends the Rule 1.8(c) prohibition to every lawyer in the firm, so a gift to Ted is treated as a gift to Rae.
Not soliciting avoids one part of Rule 1.8(c); preparing the instrument is separately forbidden.

Correct. Rule 1.8(c) forbids preparing an instrument giving the lawyer or a person related to the lawyer a substantial gift unless the recipient is related to the client. Under Rule 1.8(k), while lawyers are associated in a firm, a prohibition in Rule 1.8(a)–(i) that applies to any one of them applies to all of them. Rae may not draft a substantial gift to her partner.
It would be worse if Ted drafted it; under Rule 1.8(c) no one in the firm may draft a substantial gift to a firm lawyer.
Rule 1.8(c) isn't cured by consent.
questions.e: Rule 1.8(k): the prohibitions of Rule 1.8(a)–(i) that apply to one lawyer apply to all lawyers associated in the firm; Rule 1.8(j) (sexual relations) is personal and not imputed.

questions.area: Addressing Conflicts: Abstention, Consent, and Conflict Checks
questions.q: Lawyer Uma represents Vin and Wanda, business partners, in negotiating a lease, with both clients' informed consent, confirmed in writing. Midway through, Wanda revokes her consent because she has come to distrust Vin. What follows?
o: She may revoke, and whether Uma may continue for Vin depends on the facts.
Wanda may not revoke her consent once it has been confirmed in writing.
Uma must continue representing both, because the original consent was valid.
Uma may automatically continue representing Vin, because he hasn't revoked his consent.
Uma must report the revocation to the court before taking any further action.
oe: Correct. Rule 1.7, Comment [21] says a client who has given consent to a conflict may revoke the consent and, like any other client, may terminate the lawyer's representation at any time. Whether revoking consent precludes the lawyer from continuing for the other client depends on the circumstances, including the nature of the conflict and whether the revocation was caused by a material change.
Comment [21] says consent may be revoked at any time.
Once Wanda revokes, Uma can't represent her against her wishes; Rule 1.16(a)(3) applies to a discharge.
Comment [21] makes this depend on the circumstances; there may be a Rule 1.9 problem in continuing against a former joint client in the same matter.
Nothing requires reporting a revocation of consent to a court in a transactional matter.
questions.e: A client may revoke consent to a conflict at any time (Rule 1.7, Comment [21]); whether the lawyer may continue for other clients depends on the circumstances, and continuing against the revoking client may raise Rule 1.9.

questions.area: Addressing Conflicts: Abstention, Consent, and Conflict Checks
questions.tag: MR 1.7, Comment [19]: one client refuses to permit disclosure
questions.q: Lawyer Xan wants to represent Yolo Corp. and Zed Corp. jointly in negotiating a joint venture. To get informed consent from Zed, Xan would need to tell Zed about a pending investigation of Yolo that bears on the venture. Yolo refuses to let Xan tell Zed about it. Which statement is correct?
o: Xan can't obtain Zed's informed consent, so he can't take on the joint representation.
Xan may ask Zed for a general consent without describing the investigation.
Xan may tell Zed about the investigation, because informed consent requires full disclosure.
Xan may represent both if Yolo signs a waiver of the conflict.
Xan may represent both if he reasonably believes the investigation will come to nothing.
oe: Correct. Rule 1.7, Comment [19] says that when one client refuses to consent to the disclosure needed for another client to make an informed decision, the lawyer cannot properly ask the latter to consent. Without informed consent under Rule 1.7(b)(4), the conflicted representation can't proceed.
Consent without the material information isn't informed (Rule 1.0(e)); Comment [19] says the lawyer can't properly seek it.
Telling Zed would violate Yolo's confidentiality under Rule 1.6(a); the answer is that consent can't be sought.
Yolo's waiver doesn't supply Zed's informed consent.
The reasonable-belief test in Rule 1.7(b)(1) is necessary but not sufficient; each client's informed consent is also required.
questions.e: Informed consent to a conflict requires disclosing what each client needs to decide; if one client won't allow the disclosure the other needs, the lawyer can't properly seek that client's consent (Rule 1.7, Comment [19]).

questions.area: Addressing Conflicts: Abstention, Consent, and Conflict Checks
questions.q: Lawyer Abe is suing Acme Corp. for Client Bly. Midway through the case, Acme is acquired by Cogent Inc., a longtime client of Abe's firm in unrelated matters. Nobody could have foreseen the merger. Which statement best describes Abe's options?
o: Abe must withdraw from both representations, because the conflict is nonconsentable.
Abe may continue without doing anything, because the conflict wasn't his fault.
Abe may be able to withdraw from one of the two representations.
Abe must drop Bly, because Cogent is the older and larger client.
Abe may continue for Bly only if Cogent's in-house lawyers are screened from him.
oe: Comment [5] contemplates withdrawing from one; the clients may also consent under Rule 1.7(b).
Fault doesn't matter; a thrust-upon conflict still has to be addressed by consent or withdrawal.

Correct. Rule 1.7, Comment [5] says unforeseeable developments, "as when a company sued by the lawyer on behalf of one client is bought by another client represented by the lawyer in an unrelated matter," may create conflicts midstream. Depending on the circumstances, the lawyer may have the option to withdraw from one of the representations to avoid the conflict, with court approval where required and steps to minimize harm (Rule 1.16).
Nothing gives the larger client priority; the choice depends on the circumstances and on minimizing harm to the clients.
Screening doesn't resolve a current-client conflict; consent or withdrawal does.
questions.e: Conflicts can be thrust upon a lawyer by unforeseeable events such as mergers (Rule 1.7, Comment [5]); the lawyer must then seek consent or withdraw from one representation, with any required court approval and protection of the clients' interests.

questions.area: The Government Lawyer's Client, Conflicts, and Extra Duties
questions.q: City Attorney Dina advises the city's police department. She learns that department officials are ignoring a court order on jail conditions, which is likely to expose the city to large damages. The police chief refuses to change course. What should Dina do?
o: Follow the chief's instructions, because the police department is her client and he speaks for it.
Publicly disclose the violation to the press, because a government lawyer serves the public.
Do nothing, because Rule 1.13 applies only to corporations and other private organizations.
Report the matter up to higher authority in the city government, as Rule 1.13 requires for organizations.
Resign immediately, because a government lawyer may not work for officials who violate court orders.
oe: The chief is a constituent, not the client; Rule 1.13(b) requires her to act in the organization's best interest when he violates the law.
Going public isn't the first step; Rule 1.13(b) requires reporting up within the government, and reporting out is limited by Rule 1.13(c).
Rule 1.13, Comment [9] says it applies to governmental organizations.

Correct. Rule 1.13, Comment [9] says the Rule's duties apply to governmental organizations; when a constituent's violation of law is likely to injure the organization substantially, Rule 1.13(b) requires referring it up, here to higher city officials. Comment [9] adds that government lawyers may have greater authority to question an official's conduct.
She may withdraw if necessary later, but Rule 1.13(b) first requires reporting up.
questions.e: A government lawyer's client is a government organization, usually the agency or sometimes the government as a whole (Rule 1.13, Comment [9]); Rule 1.13's report-up duty applies, and government lawyers may have greater authority to question officials' conduct.

questions.q: As a state tax investigator-lawyer, Eli obtained confidential financial information about Fern, a private businesswoman, through the agency's subpoena powers. Eli is now in private practice. A client asks him to sue Fern in an unrelated contract dispute in which that financial information would be very useful. Fern was never the subject of any matter Eli handled personally and substantially. May Eli take the case?
o: Yes, because the contract dispute isn't the same matter Eli worked on in government.
Yes, because Fern was never his client, so he owes her no duties.
Yes, if the state tax agency gives informed consent, confirmed in writing.
No, and his whole firm is disqualified with no possibility of screening.
No, because he can't use that government information against her.
oe: Rule 1.11(c) doesn't depend on the same matter; it protects confidential government information wherever it could be used against the person.
Rule 1.11(c) protects persons about whom the government gathered information, whether or not they were clients.
Agency consent cures conflicts under Rule 1.11(a); Rule 1.11(c) contains no consent exception.
Rule 1.11(c) lets the firm proceed if the disqualified lawyer is timely screened and apportioned no part of the fee.

Correct. Rule 1.11(c) bars a lawyer with confidential government information about a person, acquired as a public employee, from representing a private client whose interests are adverse to that person in a matter in which the information could be used to the person's material disadvantage. His firm may proceed only if he is timely screened and gets no part of the fee.
questions.e: Rule 1.11(c): a former government lawyer with confidential government information about a person may not represent a private client adverse to that person where the information could be used to the person's material disadvantage; his firm may proceed with a timely screen and no fee share.

questions.q: Government lawyer Gwen is personally and substantially handling a regulatory enforcement case against Hart Co. During the case, Hart's outside law firm invites her to interview for a partnership. Gwen interviews, hoping to land the job, while continuing to handle the case. Is Gwen subject to discipline?
o: No, because she has not yet accepted the job or stopped working on the case.
No, if she discloses the interview to her supervisor.
Yes, because she negotiated with a party's lawyer in her own pending matter.
No, because the firm, not Hart Co. itself, invited her to interview.
Yes, but only if her handling of the case actually became more favorable to Hart.
oe: The Rule bars negotiating, not just accepting, employment.
Notice to a superior is the law-clerk exception in Rule 1.12(b); it doesn't apply to a government lawyer handling the matter.

Correct. Rule 1.11(d)(2)(ii) bars a current government lawyer from negotiating for private employment with any person who is involved as a party or as a lawyer for a party in a matter in which the lawyer is participating personally and substantially. Only law clerks have an exception, under Rule 1.12(b).
Rule 1.11(d)(2)(ii) covers negotiating with the lawyer for a party as well as the party.
The Rule is prophylactic; no proof of favoritism is needed.
questions.e: Rule 1.11(d): a current government lawyer is subject to Rules 1.7 and 1.9 and may not (i) participate in a matter she handled personally and substantially in private practice without agency consent, or (ii) negotiate employment with a party or a party's lawyer in a matter she is handling personally and substantially.

questions.q: After arresting a suspect in a child-abduction case, District Attorney Ian holds a press conference and says, "This monster has a long history of violence, and we have more than enough to put him away for life." Is Ian subject to discipline?
o: No, because a prosecutor may tell the public about arrests in serious cases.
Yes, because his remarks risk heightening public condemnation of the accused.
No, because the First Amendment protects a prosecutor's statements about a pending case.
Yes, but only if the statement prevents the defendant from getting a fair trial.
No, because Rule 3.8(f) applies only to statements by police officers, not prosecutors.
oe: He may describe the arrest and the charge (Rule 3.6(b)), but not inflame the public against the accused (Rule 3.8(f)).

Correct. Rule 3.8(f) requires a prosecutor to refrain from extrajudicial comments "that have a substantial likelihood of heightening public condemnation of the accused," except statements necessary to inform the public of the nature and extent of the prosecutor's action and that serve a legitimate law-enforcement purpose. Calling the suspect a "monster" and touting his record goes well beyond that, and also implicates Rule 3.6.
Gentile recognized that lawyers' speech about pending cases may be regulated under a substantial-likelihood standard.
The standard is a substantial likelihood of heightening public condemnation; actual prejudice to the trial isn't required.
Rule 3.8(f) governs the prosecutor's own statements and requires reasonable care to keep police and others from making forbidden statements.
questions.e: Rule 3.8(f): prosecutors must refrain from extrajudicial comments with a substantial likelihood of heightening public condemnation of the accused, except to inform the public of the prosecutor's action for a legitimate purpose, and must take reasonable care that investigators don't make such statements.

questions.q: Prosecutor Jo learns of new, credible DNA evidence creating a reasonable likelihood that Kyle, convicted of rape by her office five years ago, did not commit the crime. Which of the following must Jo do?
o: Promptly disclose the evidence to the court and to Kyle, and make or seek further investigation.
Nothing, because the conviction is final and the prosecutor's duties ended with the trial.
Disclose the evidence only if Kyle's lawyer specifically requests it.
Seek Kyle's immediate release, because any new evidence requires vacating the conviction.
Disclose the evidence to the court but not to Kyle, to avoid interfering with any appeal.
oe: Correct. Rule 3.8(g) requires a prosecutor who knows of new, credible and material evidence creating a reasonable likelihood that a convicted defendant didn't commit the offense to promptly disclose it to an appropriate court or authority and, if the conviction was in her jurisdiction, to promptly disclose it to the defendant (unless a court authorizes delay) and undertake further investigation. Rule 3.8(h) adds a duty to seek to remedy the conviction if clear and convincing evidence establishes innocence.
Rule 3.8(g) imposes continuing duties after conviction when new evidence of innocence appears.
The duty to disclose under Rule 3.8(g) doesn't depend on a request.
The duty to seek to remedy the conviction arises under Rule 3.8(h) on clear and convincing evidence of innocence; Rule 3.8(g) first requires disclosure and investigation.
If the conviction was obtained in her jurisdiction, Rule 3.8(g)(2) requires disclosure to the defendant, unless a court authorizes delay.
questions.e: Rule 3.8(g) requires prompt disclosure of new, credible, material evidence that a convicted defendant is innocent, to the court and (for her own jurisdiction's conviction) the defendant, plus further investigation; Rule 3.8(h) requires seeking to remedy the conviction on clear and convincing evidence of innocence.

questions.area: The Lawyer as Counselor and Neutral (MR 2.1, 2.3, 2.4, 3.9)
questions.tag: MR 2.4(b): the lawyer as third-party neutral
questions.q: Lawyer Lana serves as a mediator between two neighbors, neither of whom has a lawyer, in a boundary dispute. One neighbor keeps asking Lana, "What do you think my rights are? You're my lawyer here too, right?" What must Lana do?
o: Advise the confused neighbor of her rights, because a mediator owes duties to both parties.
Nothing, because Rule 2.4 imposes no duties on a mediator toward the parties.
Withdraw as mediator, because a lawyer may not mediate between unrepresented parties.
Tell them she represents neither of them and explain her role as a neutral.
Agree to represent the confused neighbor, so that her questions can be answered properly.
oe: A neutral doesn't represent either party; giving one party legal advice would compromise neutrality and isn't what Rule 2.4 contemplates.
Rule 2.4(b) requires informing unrepresented parties of the neutral's role and explaining it when they're confused.
Lawyers may serve as neutrals for unrepresented parties; Rule 2.4 sets the disclosure duties.

Correct. Rule 2.4(b) requires a lawyer serving as a third-party neutral to inform unrepresented parties that she is not representing them, and, when she knows or reasonably should know a party doesn't understand her role, to explain the difference between a neutral's role and a client representative's.
Representing one party in the same matter after serving as its mediator is barred without everyone's written consent by Rule 1.12(a).
questions.e: Rule 2.4: a lawyer serving as a third-party neutral must tell unrepresented parties she doesn't represent them and explain her role if they misunderstand it; she may not later represent anyone in the matter without all parties' written consent (Rule 1.12(a)).

questions.q: Lawyer Mel is retained to defend a company in an employment suit. He tells the company's general counsel to "keep anything relevant," but never identifies key employees, never follows up, and doesn't check whether routine email deletion has been suspended. Relevant emails are deleted months later. Which statement best describes Mel's role?
o: Preservation is the client's job alone, so Mel's instruction discharged his duty.
Counsel must actively oversee preservation, so Mel's lapse risks sanctions.
Mel has no duty, because the emails were deleted by routine policy rather than intentionally.
Mel is responsible only if he personally deleted the emails.
Mel must now recover the emails at his own expense or be disbarred.
oe: Zubulake places continuing duties on counsel to oversee preservation, not just to give an instruction.

Correct. In Zubulake v. UBS Warburg, the court held that counsel must issue a litigation hold, identify key players, communicate with them, monitor compliance, and make sure relevant information is preserved. A one-line instruction without follow-up isn't enough, and spoliation can bring court sanctions. Rule 3.4(a) bars unlawful destruction of evidence.
Routine deletion after a duty to preserve arises is spoliation; counsel must ensure routine destruction is suspended.
Counsel's duty includes supervising the client's preservation, not just refraining from personally destroying evidence.
Sanctions and discipline may follow, but there's no automatic disbarment or personal recovery obligation.
questions.e: Once litigation is reasonably anticipated, counsel must take affirmative steps to preserve relevant evidence: a litigation hold, identifying and contacting key players, and monitoring compliance (Zubulake); destroying or failing to preserve evidence risks sanctions and violates Rule 3.4(a).

questions.q: Lawyer Nat serves 400 document requests on the plaintiff in a simple fender-bender case, many of them asking for her medical records from childhood. When the plaintiff serves reasonable requests on Nat's client, Nat answers "objection" to every one without looking at the documents. Is Nat subject to discipline?
o: No, because the rules of civil procedure, not the ethics rules, govern discovery.
No, because objections are always permitted in response to discovery requests.
Yes, but only for the requests about the plaintiff's childhood medical records.
No, unless the court first enters an order compelling discovery.
Yes, because both his requests and his responses abuse discovery.
oe: Rule 3.4(d) makes discovery abuse a disciplinary matter too, alongside court sanctions.
Blanket objections without reviewing the documents aren't a reasonably diligent effort to comply.
The blanket objections are a separate Rule 3.4(d) violation.
Discipline doesn't depend on a motion to compel or a court order.

Correct. Rule 3.4(d) forbids, in pretrial procedure, making "a frivolous discovery request" or failing "to make reasonably diligent effort to comply with a legally proper discovery request by an opposing party." Nat did both.
questions.e: Rule 3.4(d) bars frivolous discovery requests and failing to make a reasonably diligent effort to comply with proper requests; the same conduct can draw sanctions under FRCP 26(g) and 37.

questions.q: After a jury returns a verdict against his client and is discharged, Lawyer Owen wants to call the jurors to learn what persuaded them. No law or court order forbids it. One juror, when called, says, "Please don't contact me again." Owen calls her twice more. Is Owen subject to discipline?
o: Yes, for every call, because a lawyer may never contact a juror about a case.
No, because the jury had been discharged when Owen called.
No, because he only wanted to learn from the verdict, not to harass anyone.
Yes, but only if the calls were made to set aside the verdict.
Yes, for the calls after she asked not to be contacted.
oe: Rule 3.5(b) bars ex parte contact during the proceeding; after discharge, Rule 3.5(c) permits it subject to its limits.
Discharge allows contact, but Rule 3.5(c)(2) bars it once the juror has said she doesn't want to communicate.
His purpose doesn't matter once the juror has made known her desire not to communicate.
Rule 3.5(c)(2) applies whatever the lawyer's purpose.

Correct. Rule 3.5(c) permits communicating with a juror after discharge unless (1) law or court order prohibits it, (2) the juror has made known a desire not to communicate, or (3) the communication involves misrepresentation, coercion, duress or harassment. The first call was proper; the calls after her request weren't.
questions.e: Rule 3.5: no improper influence on judges or jurors, no ex parte contact during the proceeding unless authorized, and after discharge no contact if law or court order forbids it, the juror declines, or it involves misrepresentation, coercion, duress or harassment.

questions.q: Defense lawyer Pam's client, Quentin, has admitted to her privately that he committed the robbery he's charged with. Quentin pleads not guilty and insists on going to trial. Pam plans to cross-examine the state's witnesses, test the evidence, and argue that the state hasn't proved its case beyond a reasonable doubt. Is that proper?
o: No, because a lawyer who knows her client is guilty may not contest the charges.
No, because a not-guilty plea after an admission of guilt is a false statement to the tribunal.
Yes, and she may also call Quentin to testify that he didn't commit the robbery.
Yes, because defense counsel may make the state prove every element.
Yes, but only if she first tells the court that her client has admitted guilt.
oe: Rule 3.1 expressly lets criminal defense counsel require proof of every element, whatever she knows.
A plea of not guilty is a demand that the state prove its case, not a factual assertion of innocence.
Presenting testimony she knows is false violates Rule 3.3(a)(3); holding the state to its burden doesn't.

Correct. Rule 3.1 requires a nonfrivolous basis for claims and contentions, but provides that a lawyer for a defendant in a criminal proceeding "may nevertheless so defend the proceeding as to require that every element of the case be established." Pam may not present false evidence (Rule 3.3), but she may hold the state to its burden.
Revealing the admission would violate Rule 1.6(a); nothing requires it.
questions.e: Rule 3.1 requires a nonfrivolous basis in law and fact (including good-faith arguments to change the law), but criminal defense counsel may require the prosecution to prove every element; she still may not offer evidence she knows is false (Rule 3.3).

questions.q: Lawyer Raj seeks an ex parte temporary restraining order for his client against a former business partner, who has no notice of the hearing. Raj knows a fact that significantly undercuts his client's claim of urgency, but the judge doesn't ask about it. Must Raj tell the judge?
o: No, because a lawyer never has to volunteer facts adverse to his client.
No, unless the judge specifically asks about the fact.
Yes, but only if the fact is protected neither by privilege nor by Rule 1.6.
Yes, because ex parte he must reveal material facts, even adverse ones.
No, because the former partner can raise the fact later when he gets notice.
oe: In ordinary adversary proceedings that's generally true, but Rule 3.3(d) creates a special duty in ex parte proceedings.
The ex parte duty in Rule 3.3(d) doesn't wait for a question.
Rule 3.3(d) requires disclosure of all material facts known to the lawyer; Rule 3.3(c) makes the Rule 3.3 duties apply even to Rule 1.6 information.

Correct. Rule 3.3(d) says "in an ex parte proceeding, a lawyer shall inform the tribunal of all material facts known to the lawyer that will enable the tribunal to make an informed decision, whether or not the facts are adverse." With no opposing side present, the usual adversary check is missing (Comment [14]).
The judge must decide now on complete information; a later chance to respond doesn't excuse the omission.
questions.e: Rule 3.3(d): in an ex parte proceeding, the lawyer must disclose all material facts known to him that will enable an informed decision, favorable or not (Comment [14]).

questions.q: Lawyer Sita wants to hire an accident-reconstruction expert, and also needs testimony from an eyewitness who will lose a day's wages to attend trial. Which arrangement is proper?
o: Paying the expert a percentage of any recovery, so that her fee is tied to the result.
Paying the eyewitness $5,000 as a thank-you for testimony helpful to the client.
Paying the eyewitness nothing, because any payment to a fact witness is forbidden.
Paying the expert a reasonable hourly fee and the eyewitness for her lost wages and travel.
Paying the expert a bonus if the jury returns a verdict for the client.
oe: Rule 3.4, Comment [3] notes that the common law rule is that an expert's fee may not be contingent on the outcome.
Paying a fact witness for the content of testimony is a prohibited inducement; only expenses and lost time are allowed.
Too strict. Expenses may be paid (Rule 3.4, Comment [3]), and reasonable compensation for lost time is generally allowed if it isn't tied to the testimony.

Correct. Rule 3.4(b) forbids offering an inducement to a witness that is prohibited by law. Rule 3.4, Comment [3] says it is not improper to pay a witness's expenses or to compensate an expert on terms permitted by law, while the common law forbids paying an occurrence witness a fee for testifying or an expert a contingent fee. As the outline notes, a fact witness may also receive reasonable compensation for time lost, if it isn't for the substance of the testimony and local law permits it.
A success bonus makes the expert's fee contingent on the outcome, which the common law forbids.
questions.e: Under Rule 3.4(b) and Comment [3], witnesses may be paid expenses (and, generally, reasonable compensation for lost time) and experts a fee on lawful terms, but never for the content of testimony, and no expert on a contingent basis.

questions.tag: MR 3.3(b): criminal conduct related to the proceeding
questions.q: During a civil trial, Lawyer Tom learns that his client has been secretly meeting a juror and has offered the juror money to vote for him. The client tells Tom to stay quiet. What must Tom do?
o: Stay quiet, because Rule 1.6 protects what his client told him.
Withdraw quietly, because withdrawal fully satisfies his duties.
Report the bribery to the police, but say nothing about it to the court.
Do nothing unless the juror actually votes for his client at the end of trial.
Take reasonable remedial measures, including telling the court if necessary.
oe: Rule 3.3(c) makes the Rule 3.3(b) duty apply even if it requires disclosing Rule 1.6 information.
Withdrawal may be part of the response, but Rule 3.3(b) requires remedial measures, including disclosure if necessary.
The duty runs to the tribunal whose proceeding is being corrupted; reporting to police alone doesn't satisfy Rule 3.3(b).
The duty arises on knowledge of the criminal conduct, including intended conduct; it doesn't wait for the vote.

Correct. Rule 3.3(b) requires a lawyer who knows a person intends to engage, is engaging or has engaged in criminal or fraudulent conduct related to the proceeding, such as bribing a juror, to take reasonable remedial measures, including disclosure to the tribunal if necessary. Rule 3.3(c) makes the duty apply even when it requires disclosing information otherwise protected by Rule 1.6 (Comment [12]).
questions.e: Rule 3.3(b): if the lawyer knows anyone intends to engage, is engaging or has engaged in criminal or fraudulent conduct related to the proceeding (bribing or intimidating jurors or witnesses), he must take reasonable remedial measures, including disclosure to the tribunal, overriding Rule 1.6 (Rule 3.3(c)).

questions.tag: MR 5.2(b): reasonable resolution of an arguable question
questions.q: Associate Uma believes a new matter may present a conflict of interest. She raises it with her supervising partner, who reviews the facts and concludes, reasonably though debatably, that there is no conflict. Uma works on the matter. A court later holds that there was a conflict. Is Uma subject to discipline?
o: Yes, because a lawyer is always responsible for her own violations, even at a supervisor's direction.
Yes, because she suspected a conflict and should have refused to work on the matter.
No, because only partners can be disciplined for conflicts of interest.
No, because she acted on her supervisor's reasonable resolution of an arguable question of duty.
Yes, unless she put her objection in writing before working on the matter.
oe: That's Rule 5.2(a), but Rule 5.2(b) carves out reasonable resolutions of arguable questions.
Rule 5.2(b) protects a subordinate who raises a concern and follows a reasonable resolution, even if she disagreed.
Every lawyer is bound by the conflict rules; Uma is protected only by Rule 5.2(b).

Correct. Rule 5.2(b) says a subordinate lawyer "does not violate the Rules of Professional Conduct if that lawyer acts in accordance with a supervisory lawyer's reasonable resolution of an arguable question of professional duty." Rule 5.2, Comment [2] gives a conflict question as the example.
Rule 5.2(b) has no writing requirement.
questions.e: Rule 5.2: (a) a subordinate is bound by the Rules even when following orders; (b) but she doesn't violate them by following a supervisor's reasonable resolution of an arguable question of professional duty (Comment [2]).

questions.tag: MR 5.1(a): managers' duty to have measures in place
questions.q: Law Firm Vale has 60 lawyers but no system for checking conflicts, no calendar system for court deadlines, and no training on handling client funds. No specific violation by any lawyer has yet come to light. Are Vale's managing partners subject to discipline?
o: Yes, because managers must make reasonable efforts to put such measures in place.
No, because no lawyer in the firm has yet violated a Rule.
No, because each lawyer is responsible only for his or her own conduct.
Yes, because managers are strictly liable for every lawyer's violations under Rule 5.1(c).
No, because Rule 5.1 applies only to firms with formal written policies.
oe: Correct. Rule 5.1(a) requires partners and lawyers with comparable managerial authority to "make reasonable efforts to ensure that the firm has in effect measures giving reasonable assurance that all lawyers in the firm conform to the Rules." Rule 5.1, Comment [2] lists conflict detection, deadline tracking and proper handling of client funds and property.
Rule 5.1(a) is the managers' own duty to put measures in place; it doesn't wait for another lawyer's violation.
Rule 5.1(a) imposes a separate duty on managers concerning the firm's systems.
Rule 5.1(c) liability requires ordering, ratifying, or knowing and failing to remediate; the managers' violation here is under Rule 5.1(a).
Rule 5.1(a) is what requires the measures in the first place.
questions.e: Rule 5.1(a): partners and managers must make reasonable efforts to have measures giving reasonable assurance of compliance (conflict checks, calendars, trust-account procedures, supervision of new lawyers, Comment [2]); Rule 5.1(b) covers direct supervisors and Rule 5.1(c) vicarious responsibility.

questions.area: Duties to the Firm, Changing Jobs, and Selling a Practice (MR 1.17, 5.7)
questions.q: Associate Wes is leaving Firm Yew for a competitor. Before he leaves, he wants to tell the clients he has worked for that he's moving and that they may choose to come with him. Which approach is proper?
o: Tell clients he is leaving and that they may choose, without disparaging the firm.
Say nothing to clients until after he leaves, because any pre-departure contact breaches his duty to the firm.
Tell clients that Yew will neglect their matters after he leaves, so they should follow him.
Copy all of the clients' files to take with him, so the clients' work won't be interrupted.
Tell clients that they must stay with Yew, because they hired the firm, not him.
oe: Correct. Burk Ch. 19.E explains that a departing lawyer may notify clients he has personally served of his departure and their choice of counsel (the client decides), consistent with his duty of loyalty to the firm while there. He may not mislead clients, disparage the firm, or take client files or firm property without authorization; the firm also may notify the clients.
Clients are entitled to know of the change and to choose; a neutral notice is consistent with loyalty to the firm.
Disparaging or misleading statements violate Rule 8.4(c) and breach his duties to the firm.
Files belong to the clients and the firm, not to the departing lawyer; he may move them only as the clients direct.
The choice of counsel belongs to the client (Rule 1.16(a)(3)); neither the firm nor the lawyer can dictate it.
questions.e: When a lawyer changes firms, clients choose their counsel; the departing lawyer may give a neutral notice to clients he served, must not mislead or disparage, and must respect the firm's interests and the clients' files.

questions.area: Duties to the Firm, Changing Jobs, and Selling a Practice (MR 1.17, 5.7)
questions.q: Lawyer Zara owns a title-insurance agency that operates from a separate office under a different name. A real-estate client of Zara's firm buys title insurance from the agency. The agency's customers are never told that the agency doesn't provide legal services. Are the Rules of Professional Conduct applicable to Zara's work at the agency for this customer?
o: No, because title insurance isn't the practice of law.
Yes, because she never made clear the agency gives no legal services.
No, because the agency is a separate entity with a different name.
Yes, because the Rules apply to everything a lawyer does in any business.
No, because the customer was already a client of her firm and knew she was a lawyer.
oe: It's a law-related service, and Rule 5.7 brings such services under the Rules when the lawyer fails to make the required clarification.

Correct. Rule 5.7(a)(2) applies the Rules to law-related services provided by an entity the lawyer controls "if the lawyer fails to take reasonable measures to assure that a person obtaining the law-related services knows that the services are not legal services and that the protections of the client-lawyer relationship do not exist." Title insurance is a classic law-related service listed in the Rule's Comments.
Separateness helps, but Rule 5.7(a)(2) still applies the Rules if she fails to take reasonable measures to clarify that no legal services are provided.
The Rules apply to law-related services only in the circumstances Rule 5.7(a) describes.
A firm client is especially likely to assume lawyer protections apply, which is why the clarifying measures matter (Rule 5.7, Comment [6]).
questions.e: Rule 5.7: a lawyer providing law-related services is subject to the Rules if the services aren't distinct from her legal services, or if they come from an entity she controls and she fails to take reasonable measures to make clear they aren't legal services and lack the client-lawyer protections.

questions.tag: MR 1.13(g): representing the organization and a constituent
questions.q: Outside counsel Abe represents Bolt Corp. Bolt's CEO, Cass, is sued along with Bolt for alleged discrimination, and asks Abe to represent her too. Bolt and Cass have the same defense: the decision was legitimate. Who may consent for Bolt to the joint representation?
o: Cass herself, because she is Bolt's chief executive officer.
An appropriate Bolt official other than Cass, or the shareholders, under Rule 1.7.
No one, because a lawyer may never represent both a company and its officer.
Abe himself, because he is in the best position to judge whether a conflict exists.
The court in which the discrimination suit is pending.
oe: Rule 1.13(g) requires consent from an official other than the individual to be represented.

Correct. Rule 1.13(g) allows a lawyer for an organization to represent its constituents, subject to Rule 1.7. If the organization's consent is required, it "shall be given by an appropriate official of the organization other than the individual who is to be represented, or by the shareholders."
Joint representation is permitted under Rule 1.13(g), subject to Rule 1.7.
The lawyer must reasonably believe he can represent both (Rule 1.7(b)(1)), but the clients give consent.
Courts may rule on disqualification motions, but consent to a conflict comes from the clients.
questions.e: Rule 1.13(g): a lawyer for an organization may also represent its constituents, subject to Rule 1.7; the organization's consent must come from an appropriate official other than the person to be represented, or from the shareholders.

questions.tag: Constituents in conflict: corporate civil wars
questions.q: Lawyer Dov is general counsel to Echo Inc., which is owned 50-50 by its two founders. The founders have fallen out, and each demands that Dov take his side in a fight over control of the company and its board. What should Dov do?
o: Take the side of the founder who first hired him, because that founder speaks for the company.
Represent both founders jointly, because their combined ownership equals the whole company.
Represent the company's interests and decline to act as either founder's lawyer in the dispute.
Resign immediately, because a lawyer can't represent a company whose owners disagree.
Take the side of the founder whose position he thinks is better for the company's business.
oe: Neither founder alone controls a 50-50 company; siding with one would betray the entity.
The founders' interests are directly adverse in the control fight; Rule 1.7 forbids representing them both in it.

Correct. Rule 1.13(a) makes the organization the client acting through its duly authorized constituents. Burk Ch. 23.A explains that in a "corporate civil war" between constituents, company counsel represents the entity and shouldn't take sides by representing either faction; each founder should get his own lawyer (Rule 1.13(f), Rule 4.3).
Disagreement among owners doesn't end the representation of the entity.
Choosing between the factions in their personal fight is taking sides; counsel should serve the entity and point each founder to separate counsel.
questions.e: The organization is the client (Rule 1.13(a)); when constituents fight over control, company counsel serves the entity, takes neither side, and clarifies his role to the individuals (Rule 1.13(f), Rule 4.3).

questions.q: In-house lawyer Faye reports up to the board that Glow Corp.'s CFO is falsifying financial statements. The CFO persuades the CEO to fire Faye before the board meets, and the CEO tells the board that Faye left "for personal reasons." What may or must Faye do?
o: Nothing, because her duties to Glow ended when she was fired.
Report the CFO's fraud to the press, because her firing proves the company won't act.
Sue Glow for wrongful discharge, which the Rules require before any other step.
Inform the CEO in writing that she disagrees with her firing.
She must make sure the board learns she was fired for reporting up.
oe: Rule 1.13(e) imposes a continuing duty to inform the highest authority of a retaliatory discharge.
Reporting out is limited by Rule 1.13(c) and Rule 1.6(b); Rule 1.13(e) first requires informing the board.
Whether she has a civil claim is a separate question; the Rules require informing the highest authority.
The CEO is the one who fired her; the duty is to inform the organization's highest authority, the board.

Correct. Rule 1.13(e) says a lawyer who reasonably believes she was discharged because of actions taken under Rule 1.13(b) or (c) "shall proceed as the lawyer reasonably believes necessary to assure that the organization's highest authority is informed of the lawyer's discharge or withdrawal."
questions.e: Rule 1.13(e): a lawyer who reasonably believes she was discharged, or who withdraws, because of reporting up or out must proceed as reasonably necessary to make sure the organization's highest authority learns of the discharge or withdrawal.

questions.area: Pro Bono, Appointments, and Public-Service Organizations (MR 6.1–6.5)
questions.q: Lawyer Hana volunteers at a courthouse help desk run by a nonprofit, giving short advice to unrepresented tenants with no expectation of continuing representation. She helps a tenant fill out an answer to an eviction case, not knowing that her own firm represents the landlord. Is Hana subject to discipline for a conflict of interest?
o: Yes, because her firm's representation of the landlord is imputed to her under Rule 1.10.
Yes, because direct adversity to a firm client always requires informed consent.
No, because pro bono work is exempt from all the Rules of Professional Conduct.
No, but her firm must now withdraw from representing the landlord.
No, because she didn't know of the conflict, which is what Rule 6.5 requires.
oe: Rule 6.5(a)(2) applies Rule 1.10 only if the lawyer knows another lawyer in her firm is disqualified.
Rule 6.5 relaxes the conflict rules for short-term limited services because conflict checks are impractical there.
Pro bono lawyers are bound by the Rules; Rule 6.5 relaxes only the conflict rules, and only when the lawyer lacks knowledge.
Rule 6.5(b) says Rule 1.10 is inapplicable to such representations except as Rule 6.5(a)(2) provides, so the firm isn't disqualified.

Correct. Rule 6.5(a) says a lawyer providing short-term limited legal services through a nonprofit or court program, without expectation of continuing representation, is subject to Rules 1.7 and 1.9(a) only if she knows the representation involves a conflict, and to Rule 1.10 only if she knows another lawyer in her firm is disqualified. Hana didn't know.
questions.e: Rule 6.5: in nonprofit or court-annexed short-term limited legal services, Rules 1.7 and 1.9(a) apply only if the lawyer knows of a conflict, Rule 1.10 only if she knows a firm colleague is disqualified, and her work isn't imputed to the firm.

questions.q: In settlement talks for an injured pedestrian's claim, defense lawyer Ike tells the plaintiff's lawyer, "My client's policy limit is $100,000, so that's all you'll ever see." Ike knows the limit is $500,000. Is Ike subject to discipline?
o: No, because statements in settlement negotiations aren't treated as statements of fact.
No, because Ike was speaking to opposing counsel, who could have demanded the policy.
No, because a lawyer may say whatever helps his client in negotiations.
Yes, because the size of the insurance coverage is a material fact, not negotiating puffery.
Yes, but only if the plaintiff settles in reliance on the statement.
oe: Comment [2] excludes only certain kinds of statements, such as estimates of value and a party's settlement intentions; insurance coverage is a hard fact.
The listener's ability to verify the statement doesn't excuse a knowing falsehood.
Rule 4.1(a) prohibits knowingly false statements of material fact to third persons, in negotiations or anywhere else.

Correct. Rule 4.1(a) bars knowingly false statements of material fact to third persons. Rule 4.1, Comment [2] excludes estimates of value and settlement intentions, but the amount of available insurance is a fact, and lying about it is a false statement of material fact (and fraud under Rule 8.4(c)).
Discipline under Rule 4.1(a) doesn't depend on reliance or harm.
questions.e: Rule 4.1(a) bars knowingly false statements of material fact or law to third persons; negotiation puffery about value or settlement intentions isn't a material fact (Comment [2]), but statements about facts like insurance limits are.

questions.q: Lawyer Jen represents a seller of a small apartment building. The buyer's lawyer asks whether there are any code violations. Jen answers, truthfully, "The city's last inspection, three years ago, found none," but she knows that a city notice of serious violations arrived last month. Is Jen subject to discipline?
o: No, because everything Jen said was literally true.
No, because a lawyer has no duty to volunteer facts to the other side.
No, because the information about the notice is confidential under Rule 1.6.
Yes, because a misleading half-truth counts as a false statement.
Yes, because she was required to disclose all code violations before the buyer asked.
oe: Literal truth doesn't save a statement that misleads through omission (Rule 4.1, Comment [1]).
There's generally no duty to volunteer facts, but once Jen answered the question she couldn't do so misleadingly.
Rule 1.6 might let her decline to answer, but it doesn't permit a misleading answer.

Correct. Rule 4.1, Comment [1] says misrepresentations "can also occur by partially true but misleading statements or omissions that are the equivalent of affirmative false statements." Answering a direct question with a technically true but misleading half-truth violates Rule 4.1(a).
The violation is the misleading answer, not a failure to volunteer before being asked.
