questions.e: Under Rule 4.1(a) and Comment [1], a lawyer may decline to answer, but if she speaks she may not mislead by half-truths or omissions equivalent to false statements.

questions.tag: MR 4.2, Comment [4]: parties may talk to each other
questions.q: Lawyer Kip represents a wife in a contested divorce. The husband is represented by counsel. The wife tells Kip she plans to meet her husband for coffee to talk about settling, and asks Kip to help her prepare what to say. May Kip help her?
o: No, because helping the wife prepare is communicating with a represented person through an intermediary.
No, unless the husband's lawyer consents to the meeting.
Yes, and Kip may attend the meeting and speak to the husband himself.
Yes, because parties may communicate directly, and a lawyer may advise the client about such communications.
No, because represented parties may not discuss settlement without their lawyers present.
oe: Rule 8.4(a) forbids violating the Rules through the acts of another, but Comment [4] expressly lets a lawyer advise a client about communications the client may lawfully make.
The parties don't need their lawyers' consent to talk to each other.
Kip's own communication with the represented husband would violate Rule 4.2 without his lawyer's consent.

Correct. Rule 4.2, Comment [4] says "parties to a matter may communicate directly with each other, and a lawyer is not prohibited from advising a client concerning a communication that the client is legally entitled to make." Kip may help her prepare, though he may not use her to deliver his own overreaching script designed to get around Rule 4.2.
Rule 4.2 limits lawyers, not parties; the spouses may talk directly.
questions.e: Rule 4.2 limits the lawyer's own communications; represented parties may talk to each other, and a lawyer may advise his client about what to say (Comment [4]), so long as the client isn't used as a conduit for the lawyer's overreaching.

questions.q: Before any charges are filed, federal prosecutor Lou directs an undercover informant to record conversations with a business owner under investigation for fraud. Lou knows the business owner has hired a lawyer to deal with the investigation. Do the informant's recorded conversations violate Rule 4.2?
o: Generally not, because investigative contacts before formal charges may be authorized by law.
Yes, because a prosecutor may not use an agent to communicate with a represented person.
Yes, because the business owner's lawyer didn't consent to the contacts.
No, because Rule 4.2 never applies to government lawyers.
No, because the business owner isn't represented until charges are filed.
oe: Correct. Rule 4.2 permits communications "authorized by law." Rule 4.2, Comment [5] says communications authorized by law may include investigative activities of lawyers representing governmental entities, directly or through investigative agents, before the commencement of criminal or civil enforcement proceedings, subject to constitutional limits. Most courts permit such pre-charge covert contacts.
Rule 8.4(a) normally bars doing through an agent what the lawyer can't do directly, but pre-charge investigative contacts can be authorized by law (Rule 4.2, Comment [5]).
Consent of counsel is one exception; "authorized by law" is another, and it covers this kind of investigative contact.
Rule 4.2 does apply to government lawyers; the authorized-by-law exception is what covers some of their investigative work.
He has hired a lawyer for the investigation, so he is represented; the exception, not the absence of representation, permits the contacts.
questions.e: Rule 4.2 allows communications authorized by law or court order; Comment [5] includes government investigative contacts before formal proceedings begin, subject to constitutional limits, while after charges the Sixth Amendment and Rule 4.2 restrict contact.

questions.tag: MR 4.3: correcting a misunderstanding of role
questions.q: Lawyer Mae represents a company in a wrongful-death suit. She interviews an unrepresented witness, Ned, who says, "I'm glad you're here to look out for me, since I might get sued too." Mae says nothing in response and continues the interview. Is Mae subject to discipline?
o: Yes, because she had to correct his misunderstanding of her role.
No, because she never told Ned that she represented him.
No, because Ned is only a witness, not a party to the suit.
Yes, because she must stop the interview and advise Ned not to talk to anyone.
No, because a lawyer may let a witness believe whatever makes the witness more cooperative.
oe: Correct. Rule 4.3 provides that "when the lawyer knows or reasonably should know that the unrepresented person misunderstands the lawyer's role in the matter, the lawyer shall make reasonable efforts to correct the misunderstanding." Ned's comment shows he thinks Mae represents him, and his interests may conflict with her client's.
Rule 4.3 requires more than not lying: she must correct a misunderstanding she knows about.
Rule 4.3 protects any unrepresented person the lawyer deals with on a client's behalf.
Advising him not to cooperate would be legal advice to an unrepresented person (Rule 4.3), and asking a non-client to withhold information can violate Rule 3.4(f).
Exploiting a known misunderstanding of her role is exactly what Rule 4.3 forbids.
questions.e: Rule 4.3 requires the lawyer to correct an unrepresented person's misunderstanding of her role once she knows or reasonably should know of it, and bars legal advice (other than to get a lawyer) when interests may conflict.

questions.tag: MR 1.2, Comment [12]: testing the law vs. defying a court order
questions.q: Client Ova, an activist, asks Lawyer Pip two questions: (1) whether she can refuse to pay a new city permit fee to bring a test case challenging it, accepting the fine; and (2) whether she should ignore a court injunction against her protests because she believes it is unconstitutional. What may Pip advise?
o: He may advise her to do both, because both are good-faith challenges to the law.
He may advise her on neither, because a lawyer may never advise a client to break any law.
He may advise on testing the fee by nonpayment, but should not counsel her to disobey the injunction.
He may advise on the injunction but not the fee, because constitutional rights override court orders.
He may advise on both, so long as he tells her the likely penalties.
oe: Testing a statute is permitted, but counseling disobedience of an injunction invites contempt; the order must be challenged through the courts.
Rule 1.2(d) and Comment [12] permit advice on a good-faith test of a statute or regulation.

Correct. Rule 1.2(d) lets a lawyer counsel a client to make a good-faith effort to determine the validity of a law, and Rule 1.2, Comment [12] recognizes that this may require disobedience of a statute or regulation. But Burk Ch. 13 stresses that disobeying a court order isn't a defense to contempt even if the order is unconstitutional (the Supreme Court's Birmingham march case, Walker); the remedy is to challenge it in court.
This reverses the law: an injunction must be obeyed until set aside, even if it may be unconstitutional.
Explaining consequences is always permitted, but actively counseling disobedience of a court order isn't a good-faith test of the law.
questions.e: Rule 1.2(d) permits counseling a good-faith effort to test the validity of a law, which may involve disobeying a statute (Comment [12]); disobeying a court order is no way to test it, since unconstitutionality isn't a defense to contempt.

questions.q: Lawyer Quill sets up a series of shell companies and wire transfers for a client who pays large fees in cash, won't explain the source of the money, and asks that no records mention his name. Quill deliberately avoids asking where the money comes from so that he won't "know" anything. The money turns out to be drug proceeds. Which statement best describes Quill's position?
o: He is protected, because he never actually learned that the money came from drugs.
He is protected, because a lawyer has no duty to investigate a client's source of funds.
He is liable only if the client testifies that he told Quill the source of the money.
A factfinder may infer that he knew, because deliberately avoiding the truth can establish knowledge.
He is liable because a lawyer is strictly responsible for any crime his services help further.
oe: Deliberately avoiding confirmation doesn't protect him; knowledge may be inferred from circumstances and conscious avoidance.
Whatever the duty to investigate, ignoring red flags on purpose supports an inference of knowledge, and the 2023 Rule 1.16(a) amendment adds a duty to inquire and assess.
Knowledge can be proved by circumstances; a confession from the client isn't required.

Correct. Rule 1.2(d) bars assisting conduct the lawyer "knows" is criminal, and Rule 1.0(f) lets knowledge be inferred from circumstances. Burk Ch. 13 explains the willful-blindness (conscious avoidance) doctrine: deliberately failing to learn what one strongly suspects supports an inference of actual knowledge, for discipline and for criminal liability.
There's no strict liability; liability turns on knowledge, which may be inferred here.
questions.e: "Knows" (Rule 1.0(f)) is actual knowledge that may be inferred from circumstances, including willful blindness; a lawyer who consciously avoids confirming obvious wrongdoing risks discipline under Rule 1.2(d) and criminal liability.

questions.area: Abusive Tactics, Threats, and Reporting Misconduct (MR 4.4(a), 8.3)
questions.tag: Threatening criminal charges in a civil matter
questions.q: Lawyer Rae represents a homeowner whose contractor took a $20,000 deposit and never did the work, conduct that is also criminal theft. Rae writes to the contractor, "Return the deposit within ten days, or my client will report you to the district attorney for theft." The criminal matter is related to the claim, and Rae reasonably believes both are well founded. Under the Model Rules as Burk explains them, is the letter proper?
o: It is improper, because the Model Rules flatly prohibit threatening criminal prosecution in a civil dispute.
It is improper, because any threat of criminal charges is extortion.
Likely yes, because the Model Rules don't ban related, well-founded threats.
It is proper, and Rae could also promise never to report the theft if the contractor pays.
It is proper only if the contractor is represented by a lawyer who receives the letter.
oe: That was the old Model Code rule; the Model Rules contain no such express ban.
Whether a threat is extortion depends on state law and the facts (Flatley involved demands far beyond the claim); a related, well-founded threat may be permissible.

Correct. The Model Rules deleted the old Model Code's ban on threatening criminal prosecution to gain advantage in a civil matter. ABA Formal Op. 92-363, discussed in Burk Ch. 16, says a lawyer may use the possibility of criminal charges if the criminal matter is related to the civil claim, the lawyer has a well-founded belief that both are warranted, and she doesn't try to exert improper influence over the criminal process. State extortion law (see Flatley) and Rules 4.4(a) and 8.4 still apply.
Agreeing not to report a crime in exchange for payment can itself be a crime (compounding) and improper influence on the criminal process.
Representation of the recipient is a Rule 4.2 question; it doesn't determine whether the threat is proper.
questions.e: The Model Rules have no express ban on threatening criminal charges in a civil matter; under ABA Formal Op. 92-363 it is permissible if the matters are related, both are well founded, and there is no improper influence, but extortion law (Flatley), compounding, Rule 4.4(a) and Rule 8.4 limit it.

questions.area: Abusive Tactics, Threats, and Reporting Misconduct (MR 4.4(a), 8.3)
questions.q: Client Sam tells Lawyer Tia, in confidence, that his former lawyer stole money from Sam's settlement years ago. Sam doesn't want anyone to know about the theft because it would reveal the settlement's terms. Must Tia report the former lawyer to the disciplinary authority?
o: Yes, because stealing client funds raises a substantial question about the lawyer's honesty.
Yes, because the reporting duty overrides confidentiality when the misconduct is serious.
No, because the reporting duty doesn't require disclosing information protected by Rule 1.6.
No, because Rule 8.3 applies only to misconduct that is still ongoing.
No, because a lawyer has no duty to report lawyers in other firms.
oe: It does, but Rule 8.3(c) excepts information protected by Rule 1.6, and Sam hasn't consented.
Rule 8.3(c) makes the reporting duty yield to Rule 1.6, however serious the misconduct.

Correct. Rule 8.3(c) says the duty to report "does not require disclosure of information otherwise protected by Rule 1.6." Tia learned of the theft in representing Sam, so the information is protected. Rule 8.3, Comment [2] says she should encourage the client to consent to disclosure where prosecution wouldn't substantially prejudice the client's interests.
Past misconduct is reportable; the reason Tia needn't report is Rule 8.3(c).
Rule 8.3(a) applies to any "other lawyer."
questions.e: Rule 8.3(a) requires reporting another lawyer's known violation that raises a substantial question of honesty, trustworthiness or fitness, but Rule 8.3(c) excepts Rule 1.6 information and information from approved lawyers assistance programs.

questions.q: Firm Ulm's partnership agreement says that any partner who leaves may not practice law within 50 miles for two years. Partners who retire after age 65 and receive retirement benefits are also subject to the restriction as a condition of the benefits. Which part of the agreement violates Rule 5.6?
o: Both parts, because any restriction on a lawyer's right to practice is prohibited.
Neither part, because the restriction is reasonable in time and area.
The restriction on departing partners, but not the condition on retirement benefits.
The retirement condition only, because retirees are entitled to their benefits unconditionally.
Neither part, if each partner signed the agreement knowingly.
oe: Rule 5.6(a) expressly excepts agreements concerning benefits upon retirement.
Unlike many business noncompetes, Rule 5.6(a) doesn't permit "reasonable" restrictions on lawyers who leave.

Correct. Rule 5.6(a) forbids a partnership or employment agreement "that restricts the right of a lawyer to practice after termination of the relationship, except an agreement concerning benefits upon retirement." The noncompete on departing partners violates it; conditioning retirement benefits is the express exception.
This reverses the rule: the retirement condition is the permitted part.
Consent doesn't save an agreement Rule 5.6(a) prohibits; the rule protects clients' freedom to choose a lawyer (Comment [1]).
questions.e: Rule 5.6(a) bars partnership, employment and similar agreements restricting a lawyer's practice after leaving, except those concerning retirement benefits; Howard v. Babcock shows some states allow a reasonable financial toll on departing partners, but the Model Rule bars restrictions.

questions.tag: Targeted mail is not prohibited solicitation
questions.q: Lawyer Vic reads public court filings to identify homeowners facing foreclosure and mails each a truthful letter offering to represent them. The envelope and letter are marked "Advertising Material," and no one has told Vic not to contact them. Is Vic subject to discipline?
o: No, because written solicitation is permitted unless it is false, misleading, coercive, or unwanted.
Yes, because a lawyer may not solicit people he knows need legal services in a particular matter.
Yes, because using public court records to find clients is an invasion of privacy.
No, but only because the letters were sent by mail rather than email.
Yes, unless Vic first files copies of the letters with the state bar.
oe: Correct. Rule 7.3(b) bars only live person-to-person solicitation for pecuniary gain. Written targeted solicitation is permitted (Shapero, as Burk discusses), subject to Rule 7.1 and Rule 7.3(c), which bars solicitation of someone who has made known a desire not to be solicited or that involves coercion, duress or harassment.
That defines solicitation (Rule 7.3(a)), but only live person-to-person solicitation for gain is banned outright; written solicitation is allowed.
Court filings are public; nothing in the Rules bars using them to send truthful letters.
Email and other written solicitations are treated the same as mail; the line is between written and live contact.
Some states require filing, but the Model Rules no longer do.
questions.e: Rule 7.3(a) defines solicitation; Rule 7.3(b) bans only live person-to-person solicitation for pecuniary gain (with exceptions), and Rule 7.3(c) bars any solicitation of people who have said no or that involves coercion, duress or harassment.

questions.q: Lawyer Wren pays an online company $300 for each person it refers to her who signs a retainer agreement. The company isn't a qualified lawyer referral service, and it tells consumers it will "match you with the best lawyer for your case." Is Wren subject to discipline?
o: Yes, because she is paying for recommendations, and the company's claims are misleading.
No, because a lawyer may pay the reasonable costs of advertising.
No, because the company is a business, not a lawyer, so the fee-sharing rules don't apply.
No, if the clients are told that Wren paid for the referral.
Yes, but only because the fee is not shared with another lawyer.
oe: Correct. Rule 7.2(b) forbids giving anything of value to a person for recommending the lawyer's services, except reasonable advertising costs and the usual charges of a legal service plan or a qualified lawyer referral service. Paying per signed client for a "match" that implies an endorsement is paying for a recommendation (Rule 7.2, Comment [5]) and is misleading under Rule 7.1.
Paying per signed client for a "recommendation" isn't buying advertising space; Rule 7.2, Comment [5] distinguishes the two.
Rule 7.2(b) applies to payments to anyone for recommending the lawyer.
Disclosure doesn't cure a payment Rule 7.2(b) prohibits.
The problem is paying for recommendations and misleading consumers, not the absence of a lawyer recipient.
questions.e: Rule 7.2(b): a lawyer may pay reasonable advertising costs and the usual charges of legal service plans and qualified referral services, but not for recommendations; a lead generator that "recommends" or vouches for the lawyer can't be paid per client (Comment [5]).

questions.q: In a criminal trial, the judge finds that prosecutor Xavi used peremptory challenges to strike Black jurors because of their race, and orders a new jury. Does the judge's finding by itself establish that Xavi violated Rule 8.4(g)?
o: Yes, because discriminatory jury selection is discrimination in conduct related to the practice of law.
No, because a judicial finding of discriminatory peremptory strikes doesn't alone establish a violation.
Yes, because the judge's finding binds the disciplinary authority.
No, because Rule 8.4(g) doesn't apply to prosecutors.
No, because peremptory challenges can never be the basis for discipline.
oe: It may be, but Comment [5] says the judge's finding alone doesn't establish the violation.

Correct. Rule 8.4, Comment [5] says "a trial judge's finding that peremptory challenges were exercised on a discriminatory basis does not alone establish a violation of paragraph (g)." Disciplinary authorities decide for themselves whether the elements of Rule 8.4(g) are met.
Comment [5] says the opposite: a trial court's Batson finding isn't alone enough.
Rule 8.4(g) applies to all lawyers, including prosecutors.
Discriminatory strikes can be the basis for discipline if the Rule's elements are proved; the finding alone just isn't enough.
questions.e: Rule 8.4(g) bars knowing (or reasonably-should-know) harassment or discrimination on listed bases in conduct related to practice; Comment [5] says a trial judge's finding of discriminatory peremptory strikes doesn't alone establish a violation.
